prompt: A firewall line records the source and destination addresses, the ports and the time. Which of the six questions can it NOT answer by itself?
hint: Think about the person at the keyboard.

choices.text: Where
choices.why: The line says which firewall wrote it and through which interfaces the packet passed.

choices.text: Who
choices.why: Right. It knows addresses, not accounts; another record has to say which person it was.

choices.text: When
choices.why: The time stamp is on the line.

choices.text: From where
choices.why: The source address is exactly what a firewall records.

prompt: A rule flags twelve failed logins for one account in a minute. An analyst checks and finds the user had changed their password and an old phone kept retrying. What was it?
hint: Three words, three stages.

choices.text: An incident, because a rule fired and an analyst had to spend time investigating it
choices.why: A rule firing makes an alert. An incident needs somebody to confirm that something is actually wrong.

choices.text: Twelve separate incidents
choices.why: Twelve events, grouped by the rule into one alert; none of them is an incident.

choices.text: An alert that turned out not to be an incident
choices.why: Right. A rule chose it for a person to look at, and the person found nothing wrong.

choices.text: Not even an event, since nothing harmful happened
choices.why: Every failed login is an event. Harm is not what makes something an event.

prompt: Why does the lesson say the fields of a record matter more than its format?
hint: What does an analyst do with two partial records?

choices.text: Because JSON logs are smaller than text logs
choices.why: Size is not the argument, and JSON is usually larger.

choices.text: Because a SIEM rejects any line in a format it was not configured to parse, so unknown formats are lost before anybody reads them
choices.why: Collectors take unknown formats and store them as text; the problem is what the line says, not how.

choices.text: Because a shared field, such as an address and port, is what lets two partial records be joined into one story
choices.why: Right. A format can be converted; a field that was never written cannot be recovered.

choices.text: Because the format is fixed by RFC 5424 for every program
choices.why: RFC 5424 defines the syslog envelope, not what a program writes inside it.

prompt: Match each source to what it cannot tell you.
hint: Each one is blind to something.

pairs.right: what was said in the conversation
the content of an encrypted session
traffic that never touched that machine

prompt: Why is syslog in the list of five even though it records nothing of its own?
hint: A road, not a destination.

choices.text: Because it replaces flow records on small networks
choices.why: It carries lines; it does not summarise conversations the way a flow record does.

choices.text: Because it is the format and protocol most Linux and network logs travel on to a collector
choices.why: Right. A router, a firewall and a server can all send to one collector through it.

choices.text: Because it signs and encrypts every log line on the way, so a collector receiving syslog knows that nothing was altered in transit
choices.why: Classic syslog is plain text over UDP or TCP; protecting it is lesson 3's subject.

choices.text: Because Windows writes its Event Log in syslog format, which makes it the one format every operating system in the company shares
choices.why: The Windows Event Log has its own binary format; lesson 2 shows it.

prompt: Why do most organisations not keep packet capture running everywhere, all the time?
hint: Compare the size of one connection in each source.

choices.text: It is illegal to record traffic inside a company's own network
choices.why: Monitoring one's own network is ordinary; what is captured and who may read it is a policy question.

choices.text: Once traffic is encrypted, which is most of it now, a capture records nothing an investigation could use
choices.why: Addresses, ports, sizes, timing and the unencrypted start of a session are all still there.

choices.text: It costs as much storage as the traffic itself, so flow records cover the rest
choices.why: Right. A flow record of a conversation is a few dozen bytes; its capture is everything that was sent.

choices.text: Recording packets adds a delay to every connection, and users on a busy network would notice it
choices.why: A passive capture reads a copy of the traffic; the cost is disk, not delay.

prompt: In the lab, flow records are made from the traffic crossing fw's eth0. A computer on the files network copies a large file to another computer on the same network. What do the flow records show?
hint: Where does that traffic pass?

choices.text: A summary with the bytes but no addresses
choices.why: When a flow is recorded it has addresses; here none is recorded.

choices.text: Nothing about it, since that traffic does not cross eth0
choices.why: Right. A sensor sees only what passes it; two machines on one network talk without crossing fw at all.

choices.text: The file's name, taken from the copy
choices.why: Flow records never hold content, and this one does not exist.

choices.text: One record per direction, exactly as for the SSH login, because flow records follow every conversation on the company's networks
choices.why: That login crossed eth0. This copy does not.

prompt: The syslog message format, with its priority, time stamp, host name, program and text, is defined by RFC ___.
hint: Four digits, from 2009.

prompt: Your laptop has 16 GB of memory and runs Windows. Which path does the lesson recommend for the lab?
hint: One of the three was what the course was recorded on.

choices.text: WSL2, because it is already part of Windows and namespaces work in it, so there is nothing extra to install or pay for
choices.why: Namespaces work there, but nothing in the course was recorded on it.

choices.text: Running soclab.sh in PowerShell
choices.why: It is a bash script that drives the Linux kernel.

choices.text: A cloud server rented from any provider and left running for the whole course, so it is ready whenever you are
choices.why: Possible, and paid by the hour; the lesson keeps it for when nothing can be installed locally.

choices.text: An Ubuntu 24.04 virtual machine in VirtualBox, VMware or Hyper-V
choices.why: Right. It fits, and a snapshot undoes mistakes.

prompt: What does each of the lab's four machines actually consist of?
hint: One kernel, four of something.

choices.text: A network namespace: its own interfaces, addresses, routes and firewall inside the same kernel
choices.why: Right. They share the disk and the accounts, which is why one key works on all of them.

choices.text: A small virtual machine with its own copy of Ubuntu 24.04, its own kernel and its own disk, started by the script
choices.why: That would need four installed systems; the lab is one script on one system.

choices.text: A separate user account on soc
choices.why: Accounts are shared; what is separated is the network stack.

choices.text: A Docker container started from an Ubuntu image, with its own filesystem, process list and network, managed by the script
choices.why: No image and no container runtime are involved.

prompt: `bash soclab.sh up` stops with `RTNETLINK answers: File exists`, and `ip route` shows that your computer's own network is 192.168.20.0/24. What do you do?
hint: The script and your computer want the same thing.

choices.text: Run the script a few more times, since the error comes from a race between two commands and passes once the timing is right
choices.why: The collision is still there on every run.

choices.text: Delete your computer's own route to 192.168.20.0/24 so that the lab can add its route there, then run up again
choices.why: That breaks your own network to make room for a lab.

choices.text: Install the missing package
choices.why: Nothing is missing; something is already there.

choices.text: Change 192.168.20 to an unused network in every line of the script where it appears
choices.why: Right. The lab's network collides with yours; moving the lab is the safe side.

prompt: The first `ip netns add` answers `Operation not permitted`, and you did run `sudo -i`. Where are you most likely to be?
hint: Root is not enough everywhere.

choices.text: On a machine without the nfdump package
choices.why: A missing package says `command not found`.

choices.text: On a network that already uses 198.51.100.0/24
choices.why: That collision says `File exists`.

choices.text: In a container that is not allowed to create namespaces
choices.why: Right. Many online shells are containers; a virtual machine has no such limit.

choices.text: In a lab left behind by an interrupted `up`
choices.why: Leftover machines produce `File exists` for the namespace file.

prompt: A previous `up` was interrupted halfway. What gets you back to a known state?
hint: Two commands.

choices.text: `bash soclab.sh up` twice
choices.why: The second one fails on the leftovers of the first.

choices.text: Reinstall Ubuntu
choices.why: Far more than needed; the lab lives in memory and in two folders.

choices.text: `apt install` the packages again
choices.why: The packages are fine; the leftovers are the problem.

choices.text: `bash soclab.sh down`, then `bash soclab.sh up`
choices.why: Right. down removes whatever exists; up builds from nothing.

prompt: Which field ties the sshd line, the firewall line, the flow records and the packets of the login together?
hint: It is in all four and was chosen by outside's kernel.

choices.text: The key fingerprint
choices.why: Only sshd prints it.

choices.text: The source port, 33586
choices.why: Right. Same address and same port in all four records.

choices.text: The time stamp, to the second
choices.why: The sshd line is stamped when written and the capture when the packet arrived; time alone joins the wrong things.

choices.text: The account name, ana
choices.why: Only the sshd line knows the account.

prompt: The two flow records of the login show 19 and 22 packets. How many packets did tcpdump count in one.pcap?
hint: The same conversation, seen from the same interface.

prompt: What did the packet capture show about the login that no other record held?
hint: Look at the fourth packet.

choices.text: The total bytes of the conversation
choices.why: The flow records already add those up.

choices.text: The SSH client's version, sent in clear text before encryption started
choices.why: Right. `SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_9.6p1`, readable because the handshake starts unencrypted.

choices.text: The command that was run, hostname
choices.why: Commands travel encrypted.

choices.text: The account that logged in
choices.why: The account travels inside the encrypted part; sshd's log has it.

prompt: What does the firewall's line lack that the sshd line in this lab has?
hint: Compare how each one writes the date.

choices.text: The year and the time zone
choices.why: Right. `Oct  7 04:24:43` is the old syslog format; the sshd line has `2026-10-07T04:24:40-0300`.

choices.text: The source address
The destination port
choices.why: `DPT=22` is on it.

choices.text: The name of the machine that wrote it
choices.why: It says `fw`.

prompt: The firewall used 250 bytes to record the login and the capture used 11,536. Roughly how many times larger is the capture? Round to the nearest whole number.
hint: Divide.

prompt: Order these from what happens first to what happens last, for an event that ends up in front of an analyst.
hint: A record has to exist before anything can read it.
items: a program writes a log line
syslog carries the line to a collector
a rule matches it and raises an alert

prompt: Months later, somebody asks whether a server sent 2 GB to an unknown address last March. Only one source was kept that long. Which one would answer the question?
hint: Who, whom, when, how much.

choices.text: Flow records
choices.why: Right. Addresses, time and bytes per conversation, cheap enough to keep for months.

choices.text: A firewall log of new connections
choices.why: It would show the connection started, not how much it carried.

choices.text: The server's SSH log
choices.why: It records logins, not how many bytes left afterwards.

choices.text: The packet capture
choices.why: It would answer, but the lesson's point is that it is rarely kept that long.

prompt: Match each piece of the login to the record in the lab that holds it.
hint: Each record knows one thing the others do not.

pairs.left: the interfaces the packet came in and went out of
